title: AI and Chat GPT in Language Teaching: Enhancing EFL Classroom Support and Transforming Assessment Techniques
venue: International Journal of Higher Education Pedagogies
extended_summary:
This paper discusses how artificial intelligence, especially ChatGPT-like systems, can support English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teaching and assessment. It focuses on three main areas: personalized language learning, real-time language practice, and assistance with lesson planning. The paper also examines how AI changes examination techniques through adaptive testing, automated grading, feedback, and test security, while noting ethical issues such as privacy, equity, bias, and responsible use.

The article is primarily a conceptual and position-oriented essay rather than an empirical study. It draws on examples such as Duolingo, ChatGPT use in EFL classrooms, ExamSoft, Rosetta Stone, AI writing assistants, and AI-enabled virtual reality to illustrate potential applications in language education. The intended context is EFL instruction, including classroom learning, assessment settings, and university language departments.

The paper concludes that AI can enhance instruction and assessment by making learning more personalized, feedback more immediate, and testing more efficient and secure. However, it argues that AI should complement rather than replace teachers. It emphasizes that educators remain essential for interpreting AI outputs, ensuring fairness, addressing limitations in AI-generated content, and maintaining human interaction, ethical safeguards, and equitable access.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative/essay-style article with no original experimental design, no comparison groups, and no quantitative analysis. It is useful for conceptual mapping of claims and risks, but it does not provide rigorous empirical evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no measurable effect sizes and no original outcomes; its claims are qualitative and illustrative. As a result, observed impact cannot be established from the article itself.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-style conversational AI used in EFL classrooms for real-time language practice, student questioning, and teacher support.
AI-driven language learning and writing support tools such as Duolingo, Rosetta Stone, Grammarly, and similar EFL applications that adapt practice and provide grammar/pronunciation feedback.
Automated grading and feedback for student responses, including short-answer and written EFL assignments, with grammar/spelling/coherence suggestions.
AI-powered adaptive language learning platforms that tailor lessons and practice to learner performance and proficiency, such as Duolingo and Rosetta Stone.
AI-supported instructional assistance for lesson planning, material generation, and classroom practice activities in EFL instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI and ChatGPT improve EFL speaking/practice opportunities by enabling real-time conversational practice, immediate responses, and feedback on pronunciation, grammar, and vocabulary. No original experimental effect size is reported; the paper cites case examples and prior studies to support claims of improved proficiency and confidence.
finding.measure: Language practice quality, pronunciation/grammar/vocabulary feedback, learner proficiency and confidence (descriptive/case-based)

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents AI writing assistants and automated feedback as improving written English by detecting grammar and spelling errors, suggesting revisions, and evaluating clarity/coherence. It cites a case study at New York University reporting 'substantial improvements' in written English proficiency, but no numeric effect size or sample size is provided in the paper text.
finding.measure: Written English proficiency, grammar/spelling accuracy, clarity/coherence of writing

finding.finding_summary: Automated grading and feedback are described as speeding evaluation of written assignments and providing immediate corrective input. The paper states that NLP/ML systems can identify grammar and spelling errors and evaluate coherence, but it reports no original quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Automated writing feedback and grading of written/short-answer work

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI-supported practice and adaptive assessment can boost student confidence and reduce anxiety, especially in low-pressure chatbot and adaptive testing contexts. These are narrative claims rather than measured outcomes, so no effect size or sample size is reported.

Adaptive testing is described as reducing test anxiety by matching question difficulty to ability and fostering a sense of accomplishment. The paper offers no empirical estimate, only a conceptual rationale for improved affective outcomes during assessment.
finding.measure: Test anxiety and confidence during adaptive testing

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly argues that AI reduces teacher workload by generating lesson plans, answering common questions, automating grading, and streamlining exam proctoring. Benefits are described qualitatively for tools like ChatGPT, Duolingo, and ExamSoft; no quantitative workload reduction is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading efficiency, lesson-planning efficiency, proctoring efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional benefits such as improved test security, consistency in grading, and broader access to personalized language support, but it also highlights risks involving privacy, equity, algorithmic bias, and overreliance on AI. No empirical institutional effect sizes are reported; the evidence is mainly conceptual and case-based.
finding.measure: Test security, equity/access, privacy/data security, bias, institutional adoption and governance
